Describe the curve: bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean, mean = median = mode, total area 1, tails that approach the axis without meeting it

noteBlocks.lede: Weigh a crate of eggs, measure a hundred arm spans, or time the same journey again and again, and the results pile up in one shape: a hump in the middle, falling away evenly on both sides. This lesson is about that shape, the normal curve, and the shares of it that every normal curve keeps.
can: Recognise a variable that is roughly normal, and one that is not
Use the curve's symmetry: mean, median and mode together, half on each side
Use the 68%, 95% and 99.7% shares to find ranges and the share in one tail

noteBlocks.md: Plot a lot of one measured quantity, such as arm spans or the masses of eggs from one farm, and most values sit near the middle, with fewer and fewer further out on either side. The smooth outline of that pile is the normal curve, often called the bell curve. Counts that pile up at 0, 1 and 2, and quantities with a long tail of large values, do not make it.

noteBlocks.alt: A smooth, symmetric bell-shaped curve over a horizontal axis. A dashed line runs from the peak down to the axis, labelled mean = median = mode. The two tails, each labelled, run closer and closer to the axis without meeting it.
noteBlocks.caption: Symmetric about the mean, highest at the mean, and tails that come closer and closer to the axis without touching it.

noteBlocks.stem: Which of these would pile up in a bell: 200 adults' arm spans, the numbers of brothers and sisters in 200 families, the salaries in a large company?

steps.decision: Measured on a continuous scale, and gathered evenly around the average.
Small whole numbers that pile up at 0, 1 and 2, with a tail to the right.
Most near the lower end, with a long tail of a few very large values: skewed, not symmetric.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is most likely to follow a normal distribution?
options: The masses of eggs laid by one flock of hens
The number of pets in each household on a street
The times people wait for a train that comes exactly every 15 minutes
noteBlocks.answer: The masses of eggs laid by one flock of hens
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, a mass is measured on a continuous scale and gathers evenly around the average, so it makes a bell.

twin.prompt: Which of these would you expect to make a bell-shaped distribution?
options: The lengths of rainbow trout in one lake
The number of texts each pupil sends in a day
The prices of the cars for sale on a website
twin.answer: The lengths of rainbow trout in one lake
twin.explain: Length is continuous and gathers evenly around the average length.

optionNotes.option: The number of texts each pupil sends in a day
optionNotes.why: A count with a long tail of heavy users: skewed, not a bell.

optionNotes.option: The prices of the cars for sale on a website
optionNotes.why: A few very expensive cars make a long upper tail, as salaries do.

optionNotes.option: The number of pets in each household on a street
optionNotes.why: Small whole numbers piling up at 0, 1 and 2: not symmetric, like the brothers and sisters.

optionNotes.option: The times people wait for a train that comes exactly every 15 minutes
optionNotes.why: Every wait from 0 to 15 minutes is as likely as any other, so the shape is flat, not a bell.

noteBlocks.md: The normal curve is symmetric about its mean and highest there. Its mean, median and mode are one number, with half the values on each side, and the whole area under the curve stands for all of the data, a fraction of 1.

noteBlocks.title: Why the three averages agree
noteBlocks.md: The mode is where the curve is highest, which is the centre. The median cuts the area in half, and by symmetry the two halves meet at the centre too. So the mean, the median and the mode are the same number.

noteBlocks.alt: Two curves side by side. On the left, heights: a symmetric bell with one dashed line at its peak, labelled peak and mean. On the right, incomes: a curve that rises steeply, peaks early and has a long tail to the right; one dashed line marks the peak and another, further right, the mean.
noteBlocks.caption: In the bell the peak and the mean are the same place. In a skewed shape like incomes, the long tail pulls the mean away.

noteBlocks.stem: The lengths of a batch of shoes are normally distributed with mean 26.5 cm. Find the median and the mode, and the share longer than 26.5 cm.

steps.decision: The median halves the area, and the halves meet at the mean.
The curve is highest at the mean.
Symmetry puts the same share on each side.

noteBlocks.prompt: The lengths of a batch of bolts are normally distributed with mean 48.6 mm. What is the median length, in millimetres?
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, the median halves the area, and on a symmetric curve the halves meet at the mean: 48.6 mm.

twin.prompt: Pupils' reaction times are normally distributed with mean 0.31 seconds. What percentage of pupils take longer than 0.31 seconds?
twin.explain: Half the area lies on each side of the mean: 50%.

noteBlocks.text: Why so many things are normal

noteBlocks.md: A height or a mass is the sum of many small influences, each pushing a little up or a little down. A Plinko board does the same with balls: every peg pushes a ball left or right, and the bin it lands in adds up its pushes. Few paths reach the far bins and many reach the middle, so the bins fill into a bell.

noteBlocks.stem: On a board with 10 rows of pegs, why does a middle bin fill far more than an end bin?

steps.working: An end bin needs every push the same way
steps.decision: Only one path of 10 pushes reaches it.

steps.working: A middle bin takes 5 pushes each way, in any order
steps.decision: Hundreds of different paths lead there.
So the middle fills most and the ends least: a bell.

noteBlocks.title: PhET: Plinko Probability
noteBlocks.attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
noteBlocks.task: Open the Lab screen and set the binary probability to 0.5. Start with 2 rows and drop a few hundred balls. Then add rows one at a time, up to the most the board allows, and drop a few thousand. Describe how the outline of the full bins changes.

noteBlocks.prompt: On a Plinko board, what happens to the outline of the full bins as more rows of pegs are added?
options: It comes closer to a smooth, symmetric bell
It flattens, with every bin equally full
It leans over towards one side
noteBlocks.answer: It comes closer to a smooth, symmetric bell
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 3 of See it, each row adds one more small push, and the middle bins are reached by far more paths than the ends.

twin.prompt: A ball's final bin adds up 12 small pushes, each left or right with equal chance. Which bins fill most?
options: The bins at the two ends
twin.explain: Six pushes each way can come in many orders; all twelve one way only in one.

optionNotes.option: The bins at the two ends
optionNotes.why: An end bin needs all twelve pushes the same way: one path only.
The bins are reached by very different numbers of paths, so they cannot fill equally.

optionNotes.option: It flattens, with every bin equally full
optionNotes.why: The end bins have only one path each, so they can never fill like the middle.

optionNotes.option: It leans over towards one side
optionNotes.why: With pushes equally likely left and right, neither side is favoured.

noteBlocks.text: Within one, two or three standard deviations

noteBlocks.md: The standard deviation sets the width of the bell. Every normal curve keeps the same shares: about **68%** of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about **95%** within two, and about **99.7%** within three. A value more than three standard deviations from the mean is very unusual, though not impossible.

noteBlocks.title: A check on every normal answer
noteBlocks.md: The shares check later work too: the probability above a value two standard deviations over the mean should be near 2.5%, and the probability above the mean itself exactly a half.

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve with vertical lines at the mean μ and at one and two standard deviations either side. The bands hold 34.1% between the mean and one standard deviation on each side, 13.6% between one and two, and 2.3% in each tail beyond two. Brackets above mark about 68% within one standard deviation and about 95% within two.
noteBlocks.caption: The shares in every normal curve: about 68% within one standard deviation, about 95% within two.

noteBlocks.stem: The volumes of juice in cartons are normally distributed with mean 252 ml and standard deviation 1.5 ml. Find the ranges holding about 68% and about 99.7% of the cartons.

steps.decision: One standard deviation either side of the mean.
Three standard deviations either side: almost every carton.

steps.working: Each range is centred on the mean
steps.decision: Go the same number of standard deviations down as up.

noteBlocks.prompt: Commuting times are normally distributed with mean 38 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes. About 95% of the times lie between 26 minutes and what time?
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of See it, but two standard deviations for 95%: $2 \times 6 = 12$, and $38 + 12 = 50$ minutes. The range is centred on the mean.

twin.prompt: The heights of a crop of sunflowers are normally distributed with mean 1.84 m and standard deviation 0.12 m. About 95% of them lie between what height and 2.08 m?
twin.explain: Two standard deviations either side: $1.84 - 2 \times 0.12 = 1.60$ m.

noteBlocks.md: Because the curve is symmetric, every share splits evenly about the mean. The 32% outside one standard deviation lies in two equal tails, about 16% each; the 5% outside two gives about 2.5% in each tail. A band from the mean out to one side holds half of its two-sided share. Sketch the curve and shade the region first: the picture shows at once whether the share is small or large.

noteBlocks.stem: For the juice cartons, find the share above 253.5 ml and the share above 255 ml.

steps.working: 253.5 ml is one standard deviation above the mean
steps.decision: Count the steps from the mean first.
The 32% outside splits into two tails.

steps.working: 255 ml is two above: $(100 - 95) \div 2 = 2.5$, so about 2.5%
steps.decision: Halve what lies outside two standard deviations.

noteBlocks.prompt: Marks in a test are normally distributed with mean 62 and standard deviation 8. About what percentage of the marks lie between 62 and 70?
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 2 of See it, use symmetry: 70 is one standard deviation above the mean, and the band from the mean to one side holds half of 68%, about 34%.

twin.prompt: For the same test, about what percentage of the marks lie between 62 and 78?
twin.explain: 78 is two standard deviations above; half of 95% is 47.5%.

noteBlocks.md:
Recognise a bell: a measured quantity gathered evenly around its average.
Use mean = median = mode, half on each side, and a total area of 1.
Find the ranges holding about 68%, 95% and 99.7%.
Halve what lies outside for one tail: about 16% beyond one, 2.5% beyond two.

workedExamples.stem: The heights of adult women in a town are normally distributed with mean 164 cm and standard deviation 6 cm. Find the two heights between which about 95% of the women lie.

steps.working: About 95% lies within two standard deviations of the mean: $\mu \pm 2\sigma$.
steps.decision: Pick the multiple from the percentage before any arithmetic: 68% goes with one standard deviation, 95% with two.

options: About 95% of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean
95 is close to 100, and doubling reaches it
The standard deviation is always doubled
whyMenu.explain: The figure comes from the curve itself: the bands within two standard deviations hold 95% of the area. Within one they hold 68%, so the multiple depends on the percentage asked for.

steps.decision: Two standard deviations is the distance from the mean to each end of the range.
Go that distance below the mean for the lower end.

steps.working: $164 + 12 = 176$ cm, so about 95% lie between 152 cm and 176 cm.
steps.decision: And the same distance above it for the upper end: the range is centred on the mean.

twin.stem: The lengths of the leaves on a hedge are normally distributed with mean 8.2 cm and standard deviation 0.9 cm. Find the lower of the two lengths between which about 95% of the leaves lie.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on earlier work. Two classes both have a mean mark of 60. Class A's marks have standard deviation 4 and class B's have standard deviation 12. What does that tell you?
items.skill: What a standard deviation measures (from the lesson on mean and standard deviation)

options.text: Class B's marks are more spread out
options.feedback: Yes: the standard deviation measures spread about the mean. In this lesson it sets the width of the bell.

options.text: Class B did better on average
options.feedback: Both means are 60, so neither did better on average. The larger standard deviation says class B's marks are more spread out.

options.text: Class A has more pupils
options.feedback: The standard deviation says nothing about how many pupils there are; it measures how spread out the marks are.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. A set of data has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Which value is two standard deviations above the mean?
items.skill: Stepping from the mean in standard deviations (from the lesson on mean and standard deviation)

options.feedback: Yes: two steps of 5 above 50. Ranges in this lesson are built the same way.
That is one standard deviation above the mean. Two steps of 5 reach 60.
That adds 2 rather than two standard deviations. Two steps of 5 above 50 reach 60.

items.stem: One more check on earlier work. What fraction of a set of data lies above its median?
items.skill: The median cuts the data in half (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.text: A half
options.feedback: Yes: the median is the middle value, with half the data on each side. On a symmetric curve it sits at the mean.

options.text: A quarter
options.feedback: A quarter lies above the upper quartile. The median has half of the data above it.

options.text: It depends on the mean
options.feedback: The median always has half the data on each side, whatever the mean is.

items.stem: Which statement is true of every normal distribution?
items.skill: The properties of the normal curve

options.text: The mean, the median and the mode are equal
options.feedback: Yes: the curve is symmetric about the mean and highest there, so all three averages sit at the centre.

options.text: The mean is larger than the median
options.feedback: That happens in a skewed distribution with a long upper tail, such as incomes. A normal curve is symmetric, so the two are equal.

options.text: The curve meets the axis three standard deviations from the mean
options.feedback: The tails come closer and closer to the axis but never meet it; beyond three standard deviations is very rare, not impossible.

items.stem: About what percentage of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean?

options.feedback: Yes: about 95% within two standard deviations, and about 68% within one.
68% is the share within ONE standard deviation. Two standard deviations hold about 95%.
47.5% is the share between the mean and two standard deviations on ONE side. Both sides together hold about 95%.

items.stem: Masses are normally distributed with mean 200 g and standard deviation 10 g. Between which two masses do about 68% of them lie?
items.skill: A range centred on the mean

options.text: 190 g and 210 g
options.feedback: Yes: one standard deviation either side of the mean.

options.text: 200 g and 210 g
options.feedback: That range starts at the mean, so it holds only half of the 68%. Go one standard deviation below the mean as well: 190 g to 210 g.

options.text: 180 g and 220 g
options.feedback: Two standard deviations either side hold about 95%. For about 68%, go one standard deviation: 190 g to 210 g.

items.stem: A question says that some masses are normally distributed with mean 200 g and standard deviation 10 g, and asks roughly what percentage are over 220 g. What do you need to work out first?
items.skill: Using the given mean and standard deviation

options.text: How many standard deviations 220 g is above the mean
options.feedback: Yes: 220 g is two standard deviations above 200 g, so about 2.5% are heavier. The mean and standard deviation are given; nothing needs recalculating.

options.text: The standard deviation again, using the formula
options.feedback: The standard deviation is given as 10 g; the formula is for finding it from data. Count how many standard deviations 220 g is from the mean instead.

options.text: The mean of 200 and 220
options.feedback: The mean of the distribution is given as 200 g. What matters is how far 220 g is from it, counted in standard deviations.

context.setting: Four real variables, one of them roughly normal

parts.stem: Identify the variable that is most likely to be approximately normally distributed.

options.text: The lengths of leaves picked from one oak tree
options.feedback: Yes: lengths are continuous and gather evenly around the average leaf, with fewer very short or very long ones.

options.text: The number of goals scored in a football match
options.feedback: Goals are small whole numbers that pile up at 0, 1 and 2 with a tail to the right, so the shape is not a symmetric bell.

options.text: The waiting times at a stop where a bus comes exactly every 10 minutes
options.feedback: Arriving at a random moment, every wait from 0 to 10 minutes is equally likely, so the shape is flat, not a bell.

options.text: The prices of houses sold in Belfast in one year
options.feedback: Most prices sit in the lower middle with a long tail of very expensive houses, so the shape is skewed, not symmetric.

hints: Look for a quantity measured on a continuous scale that gathers evenly around its average.
Counts, flat waiting times and prices with a few very large values do not make a symmetric bell.
parts.workedSolution: Leaf lengths are continuous and spread evenly either side of the average length, so they are roughly normal. Goals are whole numbers, the bus waits are flat and house prices have a long upper tail.

questions.solutionProgram: continuous and symmetric about its average: leaf lengths

figures.alt: Four sketches labelled A to D. A rises steeply, peaks early and has a long tail to the right. B has one peak in the middle and falls away equally on both sides. C has two peaks. D is flat across the middle with steep sides.

parts.stem: Identify the sketch, A, B, C or D, that could show a normal distribution.

options.text: A
options.feedback: A rises steeply and has a long tail to the right: it is skewed, and a normal curve is symmetric.

options.text: B
options.feedback: Yes: one peak in the middle, and the same shape on both sides of it.

options.text: C
options.feedback: Two peaks means two groups mixed together. A normal curve has one peak, at the mean.

options.text: D
options.feedback: A flat top means every value in the middle is equally likely. A normal curve is highest at the mean and falls away from it.

hints: A normal curve has one peak.
It is the same shape on both sides of that peak.
parts.workedSolution: Only B has one peak in the middle with the same shape on both sides. A is skewed, C has two peaks and D is flat.

parts.stem: Write down roughly what percentage of the values in a normal distribution lie within two standard deviations of the mean.
hints: One standard deviation either side holds about 68%.
Two either side holds most of the rest.
parts.workedSolution: About 95% lies within two standard deviations of the mean (the table makes it 95.4%).

commonErrors.feedback: 68% is the share within ONE standard deviation. Two standard deviations either side hold about 95%.
99.7% is the share within THREE standard deviations. Two either side hold about 95%.

context.setting: Masses of apples from an orchard

parts.stem:
The masses of apples from an orchard are normally distributed with mean 152 g and standard deviation 9 g.
Find roughly what percentage of the apples weigh more than 161 g.

scheme.for: 161 is one standard deviation above the mean, and $(100 - 68) \div 2$

hints: 161 g is the mean plus one standard deviation.
32% lies outside one standard deviation, split between two tails.
parts.workedSolution:
$152 + 9 = 161$, one standard deviation above the mean.
68% lies within one standard deviation, so 32% lies outside, half in each tail.
$32 \div 2 = 16$, so about 16% of the apples weigh more than 161 g.

commonErrors.feedback: 34% is the band between the mean and 161 g. The apples heavier than 161 g are the tail beyond it: $(100 - 68) \div 2 = 16$%.
32% lies outside one standard deviation on BOTH sides, the light apples as well as the heavy ones. Only half of it is above 161 g: about 16%.
84% is the share LIGHTER than 161 g. The question asks for the heavier ones, the thin tail on the right: about 16%.

parts.stem:
The masses of newborn babies are normally distributed with mean 3.4 kg and standard deviation 0.5 kg. A baby is born weighing 5.0 kg.
Identify the correct statement about this mass.

options.text: The mass is very unusual: it is more than three standard deviations above the mean
options.feedback: Yes: 5.0 − 3.4 = 1.6 kg, which is 3.2 standard deviations. About 99.7% of newborns are within three standard deviations, so this is very rare.

options.text: The mass is ordinary: it is within two standard deviations of the mean
options.feedback: Two standard deviations reach only 4.4 kg. 5.0 kg is well beyond that, more than three standard deviations out.

options.text: The mass is impossible, because the curve meets the axis three standard deviations from the mean
options.feedback: The tails come closer and closer to the axis but never meet it: a mass this far out is very rare, not impossible.

scheme.for: very unusual: more than three standard deviations above the mean

hints: How many standard deviations of 0.5 kg is 5.0 kg above 3.4 kg?
About 99.7% lies within three standard deviations.
parts.workedSolution:
$5.0 - 3.4 = 1.6$ kg, and $1.6 \div 0.5 = 3.2$ standard deviations.
About 99.7% lies within three standard deviations, so the mass is very unusual, though not impossible.

context.setting: Masses of apples from an orchard

parts.stem:
The masses of apples from an orchard are normally distributed with mean 152 g and standard deviation 9 g.
About 95% of the apples weigh between $m$ grams and 170 grams. Find $m$.
hints: About 95% lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
170 is the mean plus two standard deviations; $m$ is the mean minus two.
parts.workedSolution:
About 95% lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
$2 \times 9 = 18$ g, and $152 + 18 = 170$ g matches the upper value.
$m = 152 - 18$
$= 134$

commonErrors.feedback: That is one standard deviation below the mean, the edge of the middle 68%, so the scheme's mark for two standard deviations is not reached. For about 95% go two: 152 - 18 = 134.
152 g is the mean, so that interval covers only the upper half of the 95%, and no step of two standard deviations is taken. They go both ways: 152 - 18 = 134.

context.setting: Heights of Year 12 boys in a school

parts.stem:
The heights of the Year 12 boys in a school are normally distributed with mean 176 cm and standard deviation 7 cm.
Write down the median height.
hints: The curve is symmetric about the mean.
parts.workedSolution: The curve is symmetric about the mean, so the median is the mean: 176 cm.

parts.stem: About 95% of the boys are between $h$ cm and 190 cm tall. Find $h$.
hints: 190 is two standard deviations above the mean.
Go the same distance below it.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one standard deviation below the mean, the edge of the middle 68%, so the step of two standard deviations is not taken. About 95% needs two: 176 - 14 = 162.
176 cm is the mean: that interval holds only the upper half of the 95%, and no step of two standard deviations is taken. Go 14 below as well: 162 cm.

parts.stem: Find roughly what percentage of the boys are taller than 190 cm.
hints: Only the tall boys' tail is wanted.
parts.workedSolution:
95% lies within two standard deviations, so 5% lies outside, half in each tail.
$5 \div 2 = 2.5$, so about 2.5% of the boys are taller than 190 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: 5% is outside two standard deviations on BOTH sides, the short boys as well. The tall ones are half of it: about 2.5%.
47.5% lies between the mean and 190 cm. Taller than 190 cm is the thin tail beyond it: about 2.5%.

parts.stem: One boy is 197 cm tall. Show that this height is very unusual.

accepted: It is three standard deviations above the mean, and about 99.7% of heights lie within three standard deviations, so very few boys are this tall.

scheme.for: 197 cm is three standard deviations above the mean, beyond which lies only about 0.15% of heights

hints: How far is 197 cm above 176 cm, in standard deviations?
parts.workedSolution: $197 - 176 = 21$ cm, which is $3 \times 7$: three standard deviations above the mean. About 99.7% of heights lie within three standard deviations, so very few boys are this tall.

findTheMistake.stem: The masses of newborn babies are normally distributed with mean 3.4 kg and standard deviation 0.5 kg. Ciara was asked roughly what percentage weigh more than 3.9 kg. Her working:
studentWorking: 3.9 kg is 3.4 + 0.5, one standard deviation above the mean
About 68% lie within one standard deviation of the mean
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 counts all of the 32% as heavy babies. The 32% outside one standard deviation is split equally between the two tails, so only half of it, about 16%, lies above 3.9 kg; the other 16% are the light babies below 2.9 kg.
correction: 3.9 kg is 3.4 + 0.5, one standard deviation above the mean
About 68% lie within one standard deviation of the mean
findTheMistake.feedback: Her first three lines are right, so the method is safe until the last step. A sketch shows the slip at once: shading above 3.9 kg covers one thin tail, and a third of all babies would be far too many for it.
